cartes.avantage-comparatif.title: Comparative advantage
cartes.avantage-comparatif.text: Each country gains by specialising in what it does relatively best, even if it is worse than others at everything.
cartes.avantage-comparatif.fact: David Ricardo demonstrated it in 1817 with two countries and two goods: Portuguese wine and English cloth.
cartes.offre-demande.title: Supply and demand
cartes.offre-demande.text: The price settles where what sellers offer meets what buyers want.
cartes.offre-demande.fact: In his Principles of Economics (1890), Alfred Marshall compares supply and demand to the two blades of a pair of scissors: neither cuts alone.
cartes.inflation.title: Inflation
cartes.inflation.text: A general and lasting rise in prices: the same amount of money buys fewer things.
cartes.inflation.fact: To curb it, central banks raise interest rates: credit gets more expensive, people spend less.
cartes.protectionnisme.title: Protectionism
cartes.protectionnisme.text: Shielding domestic producers from foreign competition, with tariffs, quotas or standards.
cartes.protectionnisme.fact: Economists still debate it: protecting an industry can save jobs, but often makes consumers pay more.
cartes.main-invisible.title: The invisible hand
cartes.main-invisible.text: The idea that by each pursuing their own interest, people can serve the common good without meaning to.
cartes.main-invisible.fact: Famous as it is, the phrase appears only once in Adam Smith's The Wealth of Nations.
cartes.tragedie-communs.title: Tragedy of the commons
cartes.tragedie-communs.text: When a resource belongs to everyone, each person gains by taking a little more… until it runs out.
cartes.tragedie-communs.fact: Garrett Hardin described it in 1968 in the journal Science with a shared pasture: each herder adds one more animal, and the meadow dies.
cartes.alea-moral.title: Moral hazard
cartes.alea-moral.text: When you are protected against a risk, you may be tempted to take more risks.
cartes.alea-moral.fact: The insurer cannot see how careful its customers are: that is the textbook case. The same idea applies to banks bailed out by the state.
cartes.destruction-creatrice.title: Creative destruction
cartes.destruction-creatrice.text: Innovations replace old ways of producing: some companies disappear, others are born.
cartes.destruction-creatrice.fact: Joseph Schumpeter popularised the phrase in 1942 in Capitalism, Socialism and Democracy.
cartes.triangle-incompatibilite.title: The impossible trinity
cartes.triangle-incompatibilite.text: A country cannot have a fixed exchange rate, free capital flows and its own monetary policy all at once. It must give one up.
cartes.triangle-incompatibilite.fact: The idea is credited to economist Robert Mundell, who set it out in the 1960s.
cartes.malediction-ressources.title: Resource curse
cartes.malediction-ressources.text: Countries very rich in natural resources sometimes develop less well than countries that have none.
cartes.malediction-ressources.fact: One of its causes is called "Dutch disease": in the 1960s, Dutch gas pushed up the guilder and industry declined.
cartes.tulipomanie.title: Tulip mania
cartes.tulipomanie.text: One of the first known speculative bubbles: the price of tulip bulbs soars, then collapses.
cartes.tulipomanie.fact: At the peak, in February 1637, a bulb could fetch up to ten times a craftsman's yearly wage, according to some sources; prices then crashed within three weeks.
cartes.tulipomanie.defi.text: Tulip prices are collapsing. Who can explain the bubble?
cartes.weimar-1923.title: Weimar hyperinflation
cartes.weimar-1923.text: In Germany, prices double within days: banknotes become worthless.
cartes.weimar-1923.fact: In November 1923, one dollar cost 4.2 trillion marks. A new currency, the Rentenmark, ended the crisis.
cartes.weimar-1923.defi.text: The currency is collapsing. You need ideas that stand the test of time.
cartes.krach-1929.title: The 1929 crash
cartes.krach-1929.text: The New York Stock Exchange collapses and triggers the Great Depression, which hits the whole world.
cartes.krach-1929.fact: Between 1929 and July 1932, the Dow Jones index lost 89% of its value. It only got back to its level in 1959.
cartes.krach-1929.defi.text: The crisis starts on Wall Street and spreads to the world. You need a team that thinks big.
cartes.smoot-hawley.title: Smoot-Hawley Act
cartes.smoot-hawley.text: In the middle of the crisis, the United States raises its tariffs; its partners retaliate.
cartes.smoot-hawley.fact: Signed on 17 June 1930, the law raised tariffs on more than 20,000 products. How much it weighed on the fall in trade is still debated.
cartes.smoot-hawley.defi.text: A trade war breaks out. You need to convince countries to reopen their borders.
cartes.bretton-woods.title: Bretton Woods
cartes.bretton-woods.text: The Allies set the rules of the world's money around the dollar, itself tied to gold.
cartes.bretton-woods.fact: From 1 to 22 July 1944, 730 delegates from 44 countries created the IMF and the future World Bank.
cartes.plan-marshall.title: The Marshall Plan
cartes.plan-marshall.text: The United States funds the rebuilding of Western Europe after the war.
cartes.plan-marshall.fact: From 1948 to 1952, more than 13 billion dollars were handed out, five-sixths of it as grants.
cartes.nixon-1971.title: End of the gold dollar
cartes.nixon-1971.text: President Nixon announces that dollars can no longer be exchanged for gold: the end of the Bretton Woods system.
cartes.nixon-1971.fact: Until then, an ounce of gold was worth 35 dollars. The decision was taken without consulting America's partners.
cartes.choc-petrolier-1973.title: First oil shock
cartes.choc-petrolier-1973.text: After the Yom Kippur War, Arab oil producers raise the price of oil and declare an embargo.
cartes.choc-petrolier-1973.fact: Between October 1973 and March 1974, the price of a barrel quadrupled.
cartes.choc-petrolier-1973.defi.text: The barrel price quadruples. You need a team that can act everywhere at once.
cartes.chine-omc.title: China joins the WTO
cartes.chine-omc.text: After 15 years of talks, China joins the World Trade Organization: a turning point for world trade.
cartes.chine-omc.fact: Its membership application had been filed on 10 July 1986.
cartes.lehman-2008.title: Lehman Brothers collapse
cartes.lehman-2008.text: The American bank goes bankrupt: the subprime crisis becomes a global financial crisis.
cartes.lehman-2008.fact: It is the biggest bankruptcy in US financial history, and the start of the worst banking crisis since 1929.
cartes.lehman-2008.defi.text: Banks have stopped lending to each other. You need ideas strong enough to restore trust.
cartes.ibn-khaldoun.title: Ibn Khaldun
cartes.ibn-khaldoun.text: A historian and thinker from the Maghreb, he studies the rise and fall of states, and the role of taxes.
cartes.ibn-khaldoun.fact: His 14th-century writings are cited as the first reflections on the link between tax levels and economic activity, long before the "Laffer curve".
cartes.adam-smith.title: Adam Smith
cartes.adam-smith.text: He is often presented as the father of modern economics: he explains how the division of labour makes countries richer.
cartes.adam-smith.fact: The Wealth of Nations came out on 9 March 1776 in London. Its famous example: a pin factory where each worker does a single task.
cartes.david-ricardo.title: David Ricardo
cartes.david-ricardo.text: An English economist, he defends free trade with reasoning still taught everywhere.
cartes.david-ricardo.fact: In 1817 he published On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation, where he demonstrates comparative advantage.
cartes.karl-marx.title: Karl Marx
cartes.karl-marx.text: Philosopher and economist, he analyses industrial capitalism. His ideas inspired political movements around the world.
cartes.karl-marx.fact: Volume I of Capital came out in 1867; volumes II and III were published after his death, in 1885 and 1894.
cartes.keynes.title: John Maynard Keynes
cartes.keynes.text: For him, in a crisis, the state can revive the economy by spending when households and firms no longer dare to.
cartes.keynes.fact: His General Theory (1936) founded macroeconomics. In 1944, he led the British delegation at Bretton Woods.
cartes.hayek.title: Friedrich Hayek
cartes.hayek.text: For him, market prices carry information that no planner could ever gather alone.
cartes.hayek.fact: He received the Nobel Prize in Economics in 1974, shared with Gunnar Myrdal, whose ideas were very different from his.
cartes.milton-friedman.title: Milton Friedman
cartes.milton-friedman.text: A leading figure of the Chicago school, he sees the amount of money as the key to inflation: this is monetarism.
cartes.milton-friedman.fact: Nobel Prize in Economics in 1976, notably for his work on consumption and monetary history.
cartes.amartya-sen.title: Amartya Sen
cartes.amartya-sen.text: He shows that poverty is not only a lack of money, but a lack of freedoms and "capabilities".
cartes.amartya-sen.fact: Nobel Prize in Economics in 1998, notably for his work on famines. His ideas inspired the UN's Human Development Index.
cartes.elinor-ostrom.title: Elinor Ostrom
cartes.elinor-ostrom.text: She shows that communities can manage a shared resource together, without privatising it or handing it to the state.
cartes.elinor-ostrom.fact: In 2009, she became the first woman to receive the Nobel Prize in Economics, for her work on the commons.
cartes.esther-duflo.title: Esther Duflo
cartes.esther-duflo.text: She tests in the field, as in medicine, what really works against poverty.
cartes.esther-duflo.fact: Nobel Prize in Economics in 2019 with Abhijit Banerjee and Michael Kremer, for their experimental approach to fighting poverty.
